text:
Jacek Karpiński was a Polish computer pioneer born in 1927 whose career was defined by the development of groundbreaking computing systems in the People's Republic of Poland. Following his service in the Home Army during World War II, where he suffered a hand injury and paralysis, he returned to engineering and designed early analog computing devices, including the AAH Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics and the transistor-based AKAT-1 differential equations analyzer. His most significant achievement was the creation of the KAR-65 computer in 1968, a machine capable of 100,000 operations per second that was faster than any other Polish computer at the time, despite being built with inferior components due to financial constraints.
In 1970, Karpiński founded the Microcomputers' Construction Plant to develop the K-202 minicomputer, an innovative machine featuring microchips, memory segmentation, and high-speed processing that was technically superior to international competitors like the DEC PDP-11. Despite its technical excellence, the project failed to reach mass production, with only 30 prototypes built, due to political opposition, bureaucratic sabotage, and a lack of industrial backing from the state. Karpiński faced censorship, had his passport withdrawn, and eventually retired to the countryside. In his later years, he returned to Poland as an advisor, co-authored a novel portraying his life, and was posthumously awarded the Commander's Cross of Polonia Restituta in 2010 for his remarkable contributions to computer engineering.
